pages.name: Play it back
pages.text: The move `A = [3 1; 4 2]` sends i to `(3, 4)` and j to `(1, 2)`. The flag leans with the grid. Playing it back slides every point home. That backwards move is the [[inverse]] of A, written `A⁻¹ = [1 −0.5; −2 1.5]`.

pages.name: Turn it back
pages.task: The quarter turn `[0 −1; 1 0]` has turned the flag anticlockwise. Which matrix brings it back?
pages.why: Bringing it back means a quarter turn clockwise. That sends i to `(0, −1)` and j to `(1, 0)`. Those are the columns of `[0 1; −1 0]`.

pages.name: The target
pages.text: A sends `(1, 1)` onto the dot at `(4, 6)`, because `1 × (3, 4) + 1 × (1, 2)` is `(4, 6)`. Playing it back carries that point home to `(1, 1)`. So A then A⁻¹ leaves every point alone. That is `A⁻¹A = I`, the do-nothing matrix.

pages.name: Which undoes A?
pages.task: Which of these undoes `A = [3 1; 4 2]`? The one that does gives I when you multiply it by A.
pages.why: Multiply `[1 −0.5; −2 1.5]` by A. Row 1 by column 1 gives `1 × 3 − 0.5 × 4 = 1`. The other entries give 0, 0 and 1, so the answer is I.

pages.name: The recipe
pages.text: Swap a and d, and change the signs of b and c. That matrix times A gives `[2 0; 0 2]`. That is 2 times I. And 2 is A's determinant. So divide by the determinant to get `A⁻¹ = [1 −0.5; −2 1.5]`.

pages.name: Your turn
pages.task: What is the inverse of `[2 1; 1 1]`? Its determinant is 1.
pages.why: Swap a and d to get `[1 1; 1 2]`. Then change the signs of b and c to get `[1 −1; −1 2]`. The determinant is 1, so dividing leaves it as it is.

pages.why: For `[2 4; 1 2]`, ad − bc is `2 × 2 − 4 × 1 = 0`. It squashes the plane onto one line, so nothing can tell where a point came from. A matrix like this is called [[singular]].

pages.name: Equations as a move
pages.text: The equations `3x + y = 4` and `4x + 2y = 6` say that A carries the point `(x, y)` onto `(4, 6)`. Call that point X and the dot B, so `AX = B`. Playing it back gives `X = A⁻¹B`. So `x = 1` and `y = 1`.

pages.task: Solve `2x + y = 5` and `x + y = 3`. Here `A = [2 1; 1 1]`, and its inverse is `[1 −1; −1 2]`.
pages.why: Play the move back: A⁻¹ times `(5, 3)`. Row 1 gives `x = 1 × 5 − 1 × 3 = 2`. Row 2 gives `y = −1 × 5 + 2 × 3 = 1`.

pages.task: The loop currents are 2.5 A and 1.5 A. What flows in the shared 2 Ω resistor?
pages.why: Loop 1's current runs down through the shared resistor, and loop 2's runs up through it. So it carries `2.5 − 1.5 = 1 A`. Loop 1 checks out: `4 × 2.5 + 2 × 1 = 12`.

pages.why: a and d are both 6, so swapping them changes nothing. Change the signs of b and c to get `[6 2; 2 6]`. Divide by `36 − 4 = 32`. Times `(12, 4)` it gives `(80, 48) ÷ 32`, which is `(2.5, 1.5)`.
